title: Teen Summer Jobs Are Vanishing—Here's Why That Matters
summary: If you're a teenager hunting for a summer job, you've probably noticed: it's brutal out there. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reports 219,000 fewer teens were employed this May compared to last year. Teen labor force participation has plummeted from nearly 58% in the 1970s to about a third today. "They kind of get stuck with the short straw," says economist Brad Hershbein of the W.E. Upjohn Institute. A perfect storm of AI automation, inflation, tariffs, and global disruptions is squeezing entry-level positions. Even college graduates with loans are competing for the same roles. But for those who do land a gig, the payoff is real. Mariella Silva, 19, hustled to become a barista at Zeke's Coffee in Washington, D.C. "Every time I spend something, I'm like, oh, this is like two hours of work," she says. She's learning from older coworkers and feeling the pinch of inflation—often choosing home-cooked meals over eating out. Yet many employers hesitate to hire teens. Jesse Lauritsen, Silva's boss, notes that limited availability due to school and sports makes scheduling a nightmare. "If they can only work one day a month, there's no point," he says. The result? A growing share of 18- to 19-year-olds are "idle"—neither working nor in school. Some communities are pushing back. In Ann Arbor, Michigan, Gayle Hurn hires over 100 teens as lifeguards and swim instructors each summer. She calls them "a really important part of the infrastructure of the workplace" and invests in their development, even banning phones and coaching them through tough conversations. "It's totally worth it," she insists. For teens, the message is clear: jobs are scarce, but the experience is invaluable.
why_it_matters: A shrinking teen job market means fewer chances to learn money management, communication, and responsibility before adulthood, which can widen the gap between those who gain early work experience and those who reach college or the workforce unprepared—affecting not just wallets but confidence and career paths.

background_read: Teen employment in the United States hit its peak in the late 1970s, when well over half of 16- to 19-year-olds had a job or were looking for one—often in retail, restaurants, or summer camps.
Since then, rising school enrollment, more adults taking lower-wage jobs after the 2008-09 recession, and now automation have steadily shrunk the youth job market.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics (the U.S. government agency that tracks employment data) releases its monthly report, and the latest shows a surprising drop of 219,000 teen jobs year-over-year.

The W.E. Upjohn Institute (a nonprofit research organization named after the founder of the Upjohn pharmaceutical company) studies workforce issues; its economist Brad Hershbein notes teens are increasingly “stuck with the short straw.”

In Ann Arbor, Michigan (a college town with a strong community recreation system), Gayle Hurn’s approach—hiring over 100 teens as lifeguards and swim teachers—offers a rare counterexample, showing that with investment and structure, teen employment can still thrive locally.

perspectives.description: Landing a summer job still provides crucial life lessons: teens like Mariella Silva gain financial literacy, workplace skills, and mentors. The article shows that when employers like Gayle Hurn invest in young people, the payoff is real for both sides and can transform a community.

The collapse of entry-level jobs leaves many teens idle and risks creating a generation without early work habits. Competion from college graduates and AI automation hits the least experienced hardest, and the “short straw” analogy points to growing inequality that could have long-term effects on social mobility.

The decline isn’t just a temporary blip—it’s a structural shift. Rising school demands, the disappearance of traditional retail and fast-food roles to kiosks and apps, and an economy that rewards credentials over early work all contribute. Teens now face a “chicken-and-egg” problem: they need experience to get a job, but can’t get a job without experience.

Communities could follow Ann Arbor’s lead by creating dedicated teen employment pipelines—summer government programs, partnerships between schools and local businesses, and tax incentives for hiring minors. But to work at scale, we’d also need to rethink rigid scheduling, phone policies, and wage structures so that both teens and employers benefit.
